lesson_title: Feather, Fingernail, Hammer: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
hook_text: Your radio, your sunburn and a cancer treatment are the SAME kind of wave — moving at the same speed.
clip_script: Everything in this topic is one family of waves. All made the same way, all crossing empty space without needing anything to travel through — and all moving at exactly the same speed. Three hundred million metres every second. The breakfast radio signal, the glow of your phone screen, the X-ray at the clinic — one speed, no exceptions, no overtaking. So what separates them? Only how tightly the waves are packed. And here is the rule that unlocks everything: the shorter and sharper the wave, the harder each little packet of it lands. Radio packets brush past you like feathers all day — you never feel one. Ultraviolet packets flick like a fingernail — enough of them and your skin cells take real damage. That is sunburn. X-rays and gamma rays land like hammers, straight through skin into the cells beneath — which is why the radiographer steps behind the screen, and why gamma rays can be aimed to kill tumours. Do the division and one ultraviolet packet hits nearly seven million times harder than one radio packet. Same speed on the road. Wildly different force on arrival. Feather, fingernail, hammer — and you never memorise the dangers table again.
visual_style: A dark runway with seven glowing wave-trains racing in perfect parallel; freeze on the tie; zoom into each packet striking a surface as a feather, a fingernail flick, and a hammer blow; energy counters spin up along the spectrum.
mood: A race with a twist ending — nobody wins on speed, everything is decided by the punch.
pacing: Fast parallel race open, hard freeze on the dead heat, rhythmic three-beat feather-fingernail-hammer sequence, sharp one-line closer.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and rebuild the whole uses-and-dangers table from one idea.
